Conway-Maxwell-Binomial family for over-, equi-, under-, and super-dispersed bounded counts

Source: R/families.R
com_binomial.Rd

A two-parameter generalisation of the binomial that exponentiates the binomial coefficient by a real-valued dispersion parameter nu. nu = 1 is the standard binomial. nu > 1 under-disperses, concentrating mass near the mode. 0 < nu < 1 over-disperses. nu < 0 super-disperses, producing bimodal "all-or-nothing" mass at the boundaries. Useful when a binomial fit shows systematic lack-of-fit in either tail and the response is bounded by a known trial count.

Usage

com_binomial(link = "logit")

Arguments

link

Link function for the success probability p. Currently logit only. The COM-Binomial PMF factorises cleanly only against the canonical logit parameterisation. For that reason, probit and cloglog are not exposed.

Value

A brms::custom_family() object suitable for the family argument of mvgam() / jsdgam(). The object has an attr(., "mvgam_stanvars") attribute, which holds the Stan function-block stanvar. mvgam's setup attaches it automatically.

Distributional parameters

mu

logit-scale success probability (link = logit). Distributional regression on mu is the standard formula side: bf(y | trials(trials) ~ x).

nu

real-valued dispersion exponent (link = identity, lb = -5). nu = 1 is binomial. Distributional regression is supported via bf(y | trials(trials) ~ x, nu ~ z). The support is 0:T, a finite range. The normalising sum runs over T + 1 positive terms at every real nu, which keeps the density proper with no lower bound on it. lb = -5 is a numerical floor. The log factorial term grows with -nu. Gradients past that point are hard for the sampler. A scalar nu carries the floor as real<lower=-5> with a prior truncated to match. A modelled nu is a linear predictor and carries no such declaration, leaving nu[n] free. Hold the predictor inside the range the data resolve, roughly (-1, 4).

Default priors

  • nu ~ normal(1, 1) -- centred at nu = 1, where the trials are independent and the distribution is binomial. The scale spans the range the data can resolve. The response saturates below nu = -1 and above nu = 4. Values outside roughly (-1, 4) are barely distinguishable. Strongly under-dispersed data have nu near 3. Override with prior(normal(1, 2), class = "nu") to explore wider, or a tighter scale to pull harder toward the binomial.

Sampler notes

Two corners of (p, nu) parameter space stress HMC and should be monitored:

  • nu >> 1: the PMF concentrates on a single mode and the log-normaliser gradient saturates; max-treedepth saturation becomes possible above roughly nu = 5.

  • nu << 0 with p near 0.5: mass concentrates at both boundaries and the likelihood is invariant under p -> 1 - p, producing bimodal posteriors. Asymmetric covariates break the symmetry.

Inspect mcmc_plot(fit, variable = "nu", type = "trace") and the R-hat + ESS on both nu and the intercept; if either degrades, tighten the prior on nu or shift the design to bias p away from 0.5.

References

Shmueli, G., Minka, T. P., Kadane, J. B., Borle, S. and Boatwright, P. (2005). A useful distribution for fitting discrete data: revival of the Conway-Maxwell-Poisson distribution. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C, 54:127-142.

Conway, R. W. and Maxwell, W. L. (1962). A queuing model with state dependent service rates. Journal of Industrial Engineering, 12:132-136.

Examples

# \dontrun{
# Counts out of 10 trials, simulated with `nu = 3`. At `nu = 1`
# the family is the binomial. Values above 1 give counts with
# less spread than a binomial.
set.seed(1)
sim <- sim_mvgam(
  family       = com_binomial(),
  n_series     = 1L,
  n_timepoints = 160L,
  trend_model  = "None",
  family_pars  = list(nu = 3, trials = 10L)
)

# The denominator enters through brms's `trials()` term
fit <- mvgam(
  bf(y | trials(trials) ~ s(x)),
  data   = sim$data_train,
  family = com_binomial(),
  chains = 2,
  silent = 2
)

# The posterior for `nu` lies above the binomial's value of 1
summary(fit)
#>  Family: com_binomial 
#>   Links: mu = logit; nu = identity 
#> Formula: y | trials(trials) ~ s(x) 
#>    Data: sim$data_train (Number of observations: 120) 
#>   Draws: 2 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1; 
#>          total post-warmup draws = 2000
#> 
#> == Observation Model ==
#> Smoothing Spline Hyperparameters:
#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> sds(sx_1)     4.44      1.56     2.15     8.27 1.00      878     1102
#> 
#> Regression Coefficients:
#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> Intercept    -0.12      0.10    -0.32     0.08 1.00     2241     1410
#> sx_1         -2.96      5.75   -14.11     9.66 1.00      877      876
#> 
#> Further Distributional Parameters:
#>    Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> nu     3.11      0.39     2.41     3.93 1.00     1913     1319
#> 
#> Draws were sampled using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
#> and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
#> scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).
#> 
#> Next steps:
#>   - `pp_check(fit)`: posterior predictive checks
#>   - `forecast(fit, newdata = ...)`: out-of-sample forecasts
#>   - `loo(fit)` / `loo_compare(...)`: model fit + comparison
#>   - `conditional_effects(fit)`: covariate effects
#> Use `how_to_cite(fit)` for a methods paragraph and `methods_md(fit)` for its equations.
mcmc_plot(fit, variable = "nu", type = "areas")

pp_check(fit, type = "bars", ndraws = 50)

# }
